title: FPT versus \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)
formal: Do there exist a total computable function \(f:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} , a\) constant c, and one deterministic algorithm that decides whether an n-vertex graph contains a k-clique in time at most \(f(k)(n+2)^{c}\) on every input? Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\)?
definitions: An instance is a finite simple undirected graph G on \([n]\), encoded by its adjacency matrix, and an integer k with \(0\le k\le n\), encoded in binary. A k-clique is a set of k distinct vertices for which every pair is an edge; \(k=0\) is a yes-instance. Inputs with \(k>n\) are rejected immediately, and other malformed inputs are rejected. The parameter is k, not treewidth, degree, or the size of a supplied decomposition. Running time counts deterministic Turing-machine steps on the full input. Constants and the function f may be arbitrary but must be fixed independently of n; the exponent c must also be independent of k. FPT comprises parameterized decision problems solvable in \(f(k)N^{c}\) time, where N is their input encoding length. One equivalent definition of \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) is the class of parameterized problems reducible to k-Clique by a deterministic \(f(k)N^{c}\)-time many-one reduction whose output parameter is bounded by a computable function of k alone. This is the standard parameterized reduction convention under which Clique is \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-complete. No randomness, advice, or promise about G is allowed.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
why: This is the principal boundary question for algorithms whose exponential difficulty is confined to a small parameter. It determines the force of thousands of parameterized hardness reductions and separates efficient small-solution search from algorithms whose input-size exponent grows with the solution size.

importance.reason: The defining unresolved tractability separation of parameterized complexity, with Clique as a precise and widely used complete problem.

progress.text: Downey and Fellows develop the W-hierarchy and the completeness framework that makes parameterized Clique a canonical target for the FPT-versus-\(\mathrm{W}[1]\) question.
ETH-based reductions establish the stronger conditional obstruction to \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) Clique algorithms; the textbook develops this in its parameterized lower-bound chapters.

Bottesch studies structural and relativization evidence concerning FPT and \(\mathrm{W}[1]\), explicitly distinguishing this conjecture from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). No unrelativized separation is proved.
Lin proves constant-factor FPT approximation of Clique \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard, transferring the same central assumption to approximate search.
Chen, Feng, Laekhanukit, and Liu give a simpler combinatorial construction for the \(k^{o(1)}\) parameterized Clique inapproximability bound.
Abboud, Fischer, and Shechter improve combinatorial fixed-k Clique running times by logarithmic factors. The Algorithmica publication of 22 May 2026 retains dependence on k in the exponent of n.

status_note: Explicitly presented as the central open conjecture in Bottesch’s primary paper and the parameterized-algorithms textbook. Research through 10 September 2026 located no proof of equality or separation. Conditional lower bounds and improved fixed-k algorithms are recorded with their distinct quantifiers.

context_blocks.text: For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, \(2^{2^{k}}n^{3}\) meets the requested form, while \(n^{k/10}\) does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\) is a stronger separation conjecture than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) problem in FPT time. This is why a \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\).

sentences: A k-clique is a set of k graph vertices with every possible edge between them.
The question asks whether exact detection admits time \(f(k)n^{c}\) with a computable f and an exponent c independent of k.
Enumerating vertex subsets gives polynomial time for each fixed k, but its exponent grows with the requested clique.
An algorithm of the required form would establish \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\) and change the interpretation of many parameterized hardness reductions.
The saved review distinguishes this unconditional question from stronger lower bounds that assume ETH.
